In the college library's back corner, Jaya had a message box open and a blank line where the first sentence should be. The engineer she wanted to reach, Revati Menon, designed battery systems at the electric-scooter company Jaya dreamed of joining.
'Just say hi and ask for advice,' whispered Vinita from the next chair.
'Everyone says that. She must get fifty of those.' Jaya closed the message box and opened Revati's public posts instead. Mostly about cooling problems in batteries. Then a link: a twenty-minute talk at a conference in Chennai. Jaya put in one earphone and watched it through, taking notes.
'Okay,' she murmured at the end. 'She said the hardest part was testing in forty-degree heat. I can ask how they test in monsoon humidity. That's a real question, and it shows I listened.'
She wrote three lines. Vinita read them and raised her eyebrows. 'That sounds like someone she'd reply to.'

qa.a: It was a twenty-minute talk at a conference in Chennai.

qa.a: She felt uneasy that a plain 'hi' would be one of fifty, and wanted her message to be respectful and worth answering.

qa.a: It stands out from generic requests because it asks about her own talk, which shows real interest and respect for her time.

Hi Sahil,
You laughed at me for taking two days to send one message to that data engineer in Hyderabad. Here's why.
My first draft was 'Hello, I am a final-year student, please guide me.' Then I thought: if I got that from a stranger, what would I answer? Nothing, because there's nothing to answer.
So I read her public posts first. Most were about cleaning hospital records. Then I found a recorded talk she gave at a college fest, about how missing dates in patient files wrecked a whole model. I watched it twice.
My final message was four lines. It said I'd watched the talk, and asked one thing: how her team decides when to drop a record and when to fix it. She replied the next morning with a long answer and a link to a paper.
Two days well spent.
Divyansh

qa.a: She was likely pleased and felt respected, since the question came from her own talk, which made a long answer feel worthwhile.

Sunaina, you've been writing that message for an hour. Stop. Let me, Salma, tell you what my first mentor taught me when I was trying to reach an architect I admired.
My first letter, and it was a real paper letter then, ran to two pages. My life story, my marks, my dreams. No reply. My mentor, Kaveri madam, read my copy and laughed kindly. 'Four lines,' she said. 'Who you are. One thing of hers you genuinely liked, and why. One small request, fifteen minutes or one question. And a door to say no.'
So I wrote: I am a student in Lucknow; your library building made me want to design public spaces; could I ask you one question about its courtyard; I understand if you have no time. She wrote back in ten days and gave me forty minutes.
So. Four lines. Show me.

'Okay, Kamal, you're the engineer. Pretend.' Tarun sat on the hostel bed, phone face down.
'Fine. Hello?'
'Hi, thanks for taking the time. I'm Tarun, I wrote about your talk on water sensors.' He stopped. 'Too fast?'
'Bit fast. Again.'
Tarun said it again, slower. 'Then question one: how did you test the sensors in the field? Question two: what would you tell a student starting in this area?'
'And if I just say "hmm" and go quiet?'
Tarun's hands went cold even though it was pretend. 'Then... I wait three seconds. Then I say, "Maybe I can ask it differently," and go to question two.'
'Good. Your voice is shaking.'
'I know. That's fine. It'll shake at five o'clock too. At least I know what comes after it.'
At five, the real call began, and his voice shook for the first line only.

I'm Thomas, and before my first call with a stranger I did something that felt silly: I rehearsed it on a walk around the hostel football ground.
The stranger was Naveen, an engineer at a solar firm who had agreed to fifteen minutes. On my first lap I said my opening line out loud: 'Thanks for making time, I'm the student who asked about panel cleaning.' On the second lap I practised my two questions.
On the third lap I did the part I was dreading. I imagined Naveen going silent after my first question and let the silence sit in my head for a few steps. My stomach dropped. Then I told myself: silence means thinking, not boredom. Wait, then ask the second one.
When the call came, Naveen did go quiet after my first question. I felt the same drop, recognised it, and waited. The answer, when it came, took eight minutes.

qa.q: Where did Thomas rehearse the call?
qa.a: On a walk around the hostel football ground.

qa.q: What did Thomas feel when Naveen really went quiet, and why was it easier then?
qa.a: Thomas felt the same drop in the stomach but stayed calm, because that silence had already been imagined and a plan was ready.

qa.q: Which other approach could help Thomas before an even bigger call?
qa.a: Practising with a friend who plays the other person, since a real voice can surprise in ways a solo walk cannot.

qa.q: How might the call have felt for Naveen?
qa.a: Naveen could think for a moment without being rushed, so the answer came out full and useful and took eight minutes.

Thursday: no reply. Friday: the message still showed as unread. The window closed at midnight.

In her PG room in Gurugram, Deepika had seven drafts saved: messages to data scientists at three companies, each carefully polite. She had written the first one in March. It was now June.
Every evening she opened one, read it, and closed it again. 'They're busy people,' she told Mahima, her roommate, who was folding clothes. 'Someone with two meetings an hour doesn't want a random student in their inbox.'
'You don't know that.'
'I'd find it annoying.'
'Would you, though?'
Deepika didn't answer. She added a line to draft four and saved it again.
In July, Mahima mentioned that a senior from their college had just got an internship after a fifteen-minute call with someone she'd messaged out of the blue. Deepika looked at her seven drafts, still unsent, and felt something tighten in her chest. Four months, and not a single conversation.

'Naveen bhaiya, five messages. Zero replies. Am I cursed?'
'Show me.'
Preeti handed over her phone. Naveen scrolled for a long time.
'This one's to a biotech founder?'

'You met, like, six people at the careers fair.'
'Seven. See: Ms Pillai, 12 March, water-treatment internships, follow up 12 April. Mr Dsouza, 12 March, his team's new plant, follow up after his leave ends.'
'And this column?'
'Thank-you sent. I write to each one the same evening. One line on something they said.'
'Isn't that a lot?'

passage:
Back in my second year in Aizawl, I met plenty of interesting people and kept almost none of them. I'm Lalremsiami, and I used to trust my memory. It failed me every time.
So last year I started a plain sheet: name, date, what we talked about, and a date to follow up. After every chat I also sent a thank-you the same day, mentioning one thing I'd learned.
In August I talked to Rekha, a wildlife photographer, for twenty minutes at a book fair. That night I logged her and sent a thank-you about her tip on morning light. The sheet told me to follow up in October. In October I sent her two of my photos taken at dawn, using her tip. She replied with comments, and in December she asked if I'd assist her on a shoot in Dampa.
Twenty minutes at a book fair became my first real work.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami meet Rekha?
qa.a: At a book fair, for twenty minutes.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami seem to feel looking back at the second year?
qa.a: Lalremsiami seems a bit regretful about losing touch with interesting people and relieved that the sheet now does the remembering.

qa.q: What else could Lalremsiami do to keep the connection with Rekha strong?
qa.a: After the shoot, log it, send a thank-you with one thing learned, and set the next follow-up date.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt receiving the dawn photos in October?
qa.a: Rekha was likely pleased and flattered to see her tip used, which made her want to offer more help.

grounding: Shows a student logging each contact with a follow-up date and sending same-day thanks, which turns a short chat into lasting work.
